newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RBA says inflation outlook improves.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RBA says inflation outlook improves.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), announcing the second cut in official interest rates since mid-year, said the outlook for inflation had improved and this had increased scope for a faster rate of economic growth.

"This (rate cut) decision was taken by the board yesterday in view of the improvement in the outlook for inflation, which has increased the scope for the economy to sustain a faster rate of growth," the RBA said in a statement announcing a cut in the official cash rate to 6.5 percent from 7.0 percent.
It said one of the factors which contributed to the lowering of inflationary expectations included a relatively firm exchange rate and low inflation rates abroad.
"Slower growth of average wages in the latest figures is, however, of most significance for the board's view of the inflation outlook over the next year," the central bank said.

"The economy-wide measure of ordinary-time earnings rose by 3.5 percent over the year to the September quarter, a pace which, if sustained, is compatible with maintaining 2-3 percent inflation," the RBA said. Rates were cut to 7.0 percent from 7.5 percent on July 31 this year.
The RBA said it believed that rates policy should not impede economic growth if this growth could be achieved without threatening the low inflation objective.
"In current circumstances, with employment growth moderate and with unemployment still relatively high, the scope for stronger growth ought to be ample," it said.

The RBA, which issued the statement after its board held its monthly meeting on Tuesday, said it remained concerned about the size of executive wage increases negotiated through enterprise agreements.
There was no evidence of any slowing in private sector wage increases which are running at more than five percent, it said.

"The moderation in average measures of wages was achieved only because other employees have received relatively small rises, a situation which may not be sustainable," RBA governor Ian Macfarlane said in the statement.

"Over the past year, the bank has, on several occasions, expressed some disquiet about the rate of increase in wages and salaries negotiated through enterprise agreements and with executives," he said.
"There is clearly a need for some slowing in the wage increases produced by enterprise bargains."

Macfarlane said that if the rate cut today flowed through to mortgage interest rates as expected, mortgage lending rates would have returned to their mid-1994 low point and business rates would be less than a percentage point above their 1994
"These favourable financial developments should improve cash flows of both business and household borrowers, and provide increased impetus to spending and confidence," he said.
